title: Why Your Students Need To Play
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that boundaries and consequences alone are only a small part of effective classroom management, and that the real leverage comes from making a classroom a place students love being part of — with play as one of the easiest, most underused ways to achieve that. He describes play as critical to social and academic development, capable of developing creativity, improving emotional and cognitive health, inducing productive flow states, and even calming anxiety, all while making high standards of behavior easier to enforce. Linsin offers concrete, non-'free play' ways to build movement and creativity into lessons — acting things out, building and demonstrating, heading outside for lessons, recreating historical or literary scenes, and open-ended projects. He emphasizes that play doesn't need to happen constantly; short, sprinkled-in periods are enough to build the sense of esprit de corps that makes a classroom feel special. The article frames play as both a developmental necessity and a practical management tool.
points: Rules and consequences alone are only a small part of effective classroom management; the real leverage comes from making the classroom a place students genuinely love being in.
Play is one of the most underused tools for creating that leverage, and is critical to students' social, emotional, cognitive, and physical development.
Play readily induces flow states, calms anxiety, and improves cognitive and physical health, beyond its social benefits.
Structured play — acting things out, building/demonstrating, outdoor lessons, historical or literary recreations, open-ended projects — avoids the pitfalls of unstructured 'free' play.
Play does not need to happen constantly; short, occasional periods of play, within clearly defended boundaries, are enough to build strong classroom culture.
quotes: But the truth is, there is no magic in the classroom management plan itself. The magic is in making it meaningful to your students.
One of the easiest and most rewarding ways to accomplish this is to include more opportunities for play.

Play develops creativity more effectively than any other teaching method. It improves emotional, cognitive, and physical health and teaches students how to be curious self-starters and tenacious problem-solvers.

It readily pulls students into a state of flow, which is proven to be among the most pleasurable human experiences—where time distorts, awareness heightens, and engrossment becomes so intense that they get lost in the moment.

Done right, and within a classroom with clearly defined and faithfully defended boundaries, it can allow you to ask virtually anything of your class—polite behavior, rapt attentiveness, perfect routines—and get it.
Short periods of play sprinkled here and there go a long way toward providing that certain esprit de corps.
